events.title: The amnesty in the temple of Tellus
events.summary: Two days after the murder the consul Antony convened the senate. On Cicero's motion, citing the Athenian amnesty of 403, the assassins were granted immunity, while all Caesar's acts and appointments were confirmed, since half the senators owed their offices or provinces to them. The liberators came down from the Capitol, with Antony's and Lepidus' sons as hostages, and dined with Antony and Lepidus.

events.title: Caesar's will and funeral
events.summary: Caesar's will, opened at Antony's house, adopted his great-nephew Gaius Octavius as son and heir to three quarters of his estate, left his gardens across the Tiber to the people and 300 sesterces to every citizen, and named Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins, as a secondary heir. At the funeral Antony's speech and the display of the bloodied toga, perhaps with a wax effigy showing the wounds, turned the crowd: they cremated the body in the Forum on a pyre of benches and set off to burn the conspirators' houses.
events.detail: The poet Helvius Cinna was torn apart in mistake for the praetor Cornelius Cinna. Suetonius says foreign communities mourned, above all the Jews, who came to the pyre for nights. An altar and column were set up on the spot; the temple of the Deified Julius later rose there. Within weeks the assassins had to leave Rome.

events.title: Octavian accepts Caesar's inheritance
events.summary: The 18-year-old Gaius Octavius, studying at Apollonia, crossed to Italy against his family's advice, accepted the adoption and took the name Gaius Julius Caesar. When Antony stalled over handing over Caesar's funds, he paid Caesar's legacies to the people from his own and borrowed money and courted Caesar's veterans.
events.detail: Cicero, who met him in April, thought him devoted to himself; he wrote to Atticus that the boy's own followers called him Caesar but his stepfather Philippus did not, so neither did Cicero. Moderns call him Octavian, a name he never used.

events.title: The comet of 44 BC (sidus Iulium)
events.summary: During the games Octavian gave in late July in honour of Caesar's victories, a bright comet was seen for seven days. Octavian proclaimed it Caesar's soul received among the gods, set a star on the head of his statue and put it on his coins; he privately took it as his own sign, according to his memoirs quoted by Pliny.
events.detail: Chinese records in the Han shu note a comet in the same year. It became a central image of Augustan ideology (Virgil, Horace, Ovid).
events.locName: Rome, during the Ludi Victoriae Caesaris
scholarship: Ramsey & Licht, The Comet of 44 B.C. and Caesar's Funeral Games (1997)

events.title: The cold years after Caesar's death
events.summary: Ancient writers report a dimmed sun, failed harvests and famine in the years after Caesar's murder. Greenland ice cores show that a huge eruption of the Okmok volcano in Alaska in early 43, following an Etna eruption in 44, made 43-42 among the coldest years in the northern hemisphere of the last 2,500 years; Egyptian Nile floods also failed.
events.detail: Plutarch, Virgil and Pliny describe the sun's pallor through the year after the Ides as a portent; the volcanic explanation, published in 2020, ties the political crisis to a climate shock that worsened food shortages in Italy and Egypt during the triumviral wars.
events.locName: Italy and the Mediterranean (eruption site: Okmok volcano, Aleutians)

events.title: Cicero's Philippics
events.summary: On 2 September 44 Cicero delivered the first of fourteen speeches against Antony, which he named after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon. The Second Philippic, a pamphlet never delivered, savaged Antony's private life. Through the winter of 44-43 Cicero led the senate in backing Octavian and Decimus Brutus against Antony.
events.detail: Cicero described his strategy, in a quip that reached Octavian, as to praise the young man, honour him and remove him (tollere means both 'raise' and 'get rid of'). The speeches cost him his life.

events.title: Battle of Forum Gallorum
events.summary: Antony, besieging Decimus Brutus in Mutina, ambushed the consul Pansa's army of recruits marching to join Hirtius and Octavian. The veteran Martian legion fought him to a standstill in the marshes; Pansa was mortally wounded. Late in the day Hirtius arrived with fresh troops and routed Antony's exhausted army.
events.detail: The legate Servius Sulpicius Galba's eyewitness letter to Cicero (Fam. 10.30) is one of the very few first-hand battle accounts from a Roman officer outside Caesar. Octavian, defending the camp, was hailed imperator.

sides.strength: Pansa's 4 recruit legions, Martian legion and Hirtius' relief

battle.significance: Checked Antony but cost the senate one consul.

events.title: Battle of Mutina
events.summary: A week later Hirtius and Octavian attacked Antony's siege lines; Hirtius was killed inside Antony's camp, but Antony abandoned the siege and retreated over the Alps. Pansa died of his wounds. Rumour said Octavian had both consuls killed; the senate voted Decimus Brutus the command and snubbed Octavian.
events.detail: Within weeks Lepidus, Pollio and Plancus, governors of the western provinces, joined Antony, and Decimus Brutus, deserted by his troops, was killed by a Gallic chieftain on Antony's orders.

sides.strength: Hirtius' and Octavian's armies, Decimus Brutus' garrison

battle.significance: Senatorial victory that collapsed within months; left Octavian with the only intact army in Italy.

events.title: Octavian marches on Rome and becomes consul
events.summary: When the senate refused him a consulship, Octavian, aged nineteen, marched on Rome with eight legions; a centurion delegation had told the senate, patting his sword, that this would make him consul. He was elected on 19 August with his cousin Quintus Pedius; a lex curiata ratified his adoption, and the lex Pedia set up a court that condemned Caesar's assassins in absence.
events.detail: Suetonius and Appian say twelve vultures appeared at his first auspices, as for Romulus. The anniversary, 19 August, was also the day he died in AD 14.

events.title: The meeting at Bononia
events.summary: Antony, Lepidus and Octavian met for two days on a small river island near Bononia, guarded by their armies, and agreed to form a legal triumvirate for five years, divide the western provinces, take vengeance on Caesar's murderers and proscribe their enemies. Octavian was betrothed to Antony's stepdaughter Clodia.
events.locName: island in a river near Bononia (Bologna)

events.title: Lex Titia: the Second Triumvirate
events.summary: The tribune Publius Titius carried a law, passed the day it was proposed, making Antony, Lepidus and Octavian triumviri rei publicae constituendae, three men for restoring the state, with consular power for five years to 31 December 38, the right to appoint magistrates and to issue binding edicts. Antony took the Gauls, Lepidus Spain and Narbonensis, Octavian Africa, Sicily and Sardinia.
events.detail: Unlike the informal pact of 60, this was a legally constituted college, a dictatorship in three persons. Renewed at Tarentum in 37 for a second five years, it is the bridge between the Republic and the Principate. Whether the powers lapsed at the end of 33 or continued until laid down was debated by contemporaries and is debated now.
events.debate: Whether the triumvirs' powers ended on 31 December 33 or persisted until resigned.

events.title: The triumviral proscriptions
events.summary: The triumvirs posted lists of men to be killed and their property confiscated, to raise money for the war against Brutus and Cassius as much as for revenge: Appian gives some 300 senators and 2,000 equites. Bounties were 100,000 sesterces for a free killer, 40,000 and freedom for a slave. Each triumvir sacrificed relatives: Antony's uncle Lucius Caesar, Lepidus' brother Paullus.
events.detail: Appian's fourth book collects stories of betrayal and loyalty, slaves who died for masters and wives who hid husbands; the inscription known as the Laudatio Turiae (CIL VI 1527) is a husband's real tribute to a wife who saved him and confronted Lepidus. When a levy was imposed on 1,400 rich women, Hortensia, daughter of the orator, protested in the Forum and the number was cut to 400. Varro survived; Verres did not.
scholarship: Hinard, Les proscriptions de la Rome républicaine (1985)

events.title: Murder of Cicero
events.summary: Proscribed at Antony's insistence, Cicero dithered between flight and staying, and was overtaken near his villa at Formiae by a squad under the centurion Herennius and the tribune Popillius Laenas, whom he had once defended. He leaned out of his litter and offered his neck. His head and the hands that wrote the Philippics were nailed to the Rostra; Dio says Fulvia pierced the tongue with her hairpin.
events.detail: Livy's verdict, preserved by the elder Seneca, was that he had borne none of his misfortunes as a man should except his death. Plutarch says Augustus, years later, found a grandson reading Cicero, took the book, and handed it back calling him a learned man and a lover of his country.

events.title: Deification of Julius Caesar
events.summary: The senate and people declared Caesar a god, Divus Iulius, and voted a temple on the site of his cremation. His statue could no longer be carried in family funerals; his birthday became a festival. Octavian became divi filius, son of a god.

events.title: Siege of Xanthus
events.summary: Raising money and troops in the East, Brutus besieged Xanthus, whose citizens refused to pay. When the Romans broke in, the Xanthians burned their city and killed themselves and their families, as their ancestors had done before the Persians in 546. Cassius meanwhile took Rhodes, extracting 8,500 talents.

battle.significance: Showed the ruthless fund-raising of the liberators in Asia.

events.note: Xanthus is listed under the generic 'rome' polity as a free Lycian city in the Roman orbit.

events.title: First Battle of Philippi
events.summary: Brutus and Cassius held strong camps astride the Via Egnatia with the sea at their backs; Antony built a causeway through the marsh to outflank Cassius. When Cassius attacked the works, Antony stormed Cassius' camp; meanwhile Brutus' men overran Octavian's camp, the sick Octavian having been carried out, he later said, because of his doctor's dream. Cassius, short-sighted and misinformed that Brutus too had lost, had his freedman Pindarus kill him.
events.detail: Pliny says Octavian hid for three days in the marsh. The same day the liberators' fleet destroyed triumviral reinforcements crossing the Adriatic. Brutus called Cassius the last of the Romans. The date of the first battle is not securely attested; early October is likely.

battle.significance: Each side took one camp; Cassius' death left Brutus in sole command.

events.title: Second Battle of Philippi
events.summary: Three weeks later, with his officers restless and his supply secure but his men deserting, Brutus offered battle. After hard fighting Antony's legions broke his line. Brutus fell on his sword held by his friend Strato. Antony covered the body with his own purple cloak; Octavian, says Suetonius, sent the head to Rome to be thrown at the feet of Caesar's statue.
events.detail: Messalla and Horace, a military tribune who later joked that he threw away his shield, were among the survivors. The liberators' cause died here. The victors divided the empire: Antony took the East, Octavian the thankless task of settling 100,000 veterans on land confiscated from eighteen Italian towns.

battle.significance: Ended republican resistance; Antony became the dominant figure in the Roman world.

events.title: Cleopatra meets Antony at Tarsus
events.summary: Summoned to answer for help allegedly given to Cassius, Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus to Tarsus in a gilded barge with purple sails and silver oars, dressed as Aphrodite, and invited Antony to dine. At her request he had her sister Arsinoe dragged from the temple of Artemis at Ephesus and killed, and spent the winter of 41-40 with her in Alexandria.
events.detail: Plutarch's description, followed by Shakespeare almost word for word, is the most famous set piece in his Lives. The alliance gave Antony Egypt's wealth and Cleopatra Roman protection.

events.title: Siege of Perusia
events.summary: The consul Lucius Antonius, Antony's brother, and Fulvia, Antony's wife, championed Italian landowners dispossessed for Octavian's veteran settlements. Octavian, Agrippa and Salvidienus Rufus penned Lucius in Perusia and starved it through the winter of 41-40. Lucius surrendered and was spared; the town was burned.
events.detail: Lead sling bullets from the siege carry obscene messages aimed at Fulvia and Octavian. Suetonius and Dio report that 300 senators and equites were sacrificed at an altar to the Deified Julius on the Ides of March 40, the 'Perusine altars'; many modern historians doubt it as hostile propaganda. Fulvia fled to Greece and died at Sicyon.

battle.significance: Gave Octavian control of Italy and the western legions.

events.title: Parthian invasion of Syria and Asia Minor
events.summary: The Parthian prince Pacorus and Quintus Labienus, son of Caesar's general and once Brutus' envoy to Parthia, overran Syria, killing its governor Decidius Saxa. Labienus swept through Asia Minor to Caria, styling himself imperator Parthicus on his coins. Pacorus took Jerusalem and installed the Hasmonean Antigonus as king; Herod fled to Rome, where the senate, at Antony's and Octavian's request, named him king of Judaea.

events.title: Treaty of Brundisium
events.summary: Antony returned to Italy and was refused entry at Brundisium; the soldiers of both sides refused to fight. Mediated by Maecenas, Pollio and Cocceius Nerva, the triumvirs divided the empire at Scodra in Illyricum, Antony taking the East and Octavian the West, Lepidus keeping Africa. Antony married Octavian's widowed sister Octavia.
events.detail: Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, prophesying a golden age to begin with the birth of a child in Pollio's consulship, belongs to the hope of this peace. Salvidienus Rufus, revealed by Antony as having offered to defect, was condemned by the senate.

events.title: Treaty of Misenum
events.summary: Starved by Sextus Pompey's blockade, Italy forced the triumvirs to negotiate. Sextus was granted Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Peloponnese for five years, a future consulship and augurate, and an amnesty for the proscribed who had fled to him (except Caesar's murderers). The parties celebrated with banquets aboard Sextus' flagship.
events.detail: Sextus' admiral Menas whispered that he could cut the anchor cable and make Sextus master of the world; Sextus replied that he should have done it without asking. The peace broke down within a year.

events.title: Battle of the Cilician Gates and Mount Amanus
events.summary: Antony's legate Publius Ventidius Bassus, a muleteer's son once paraded as a child captive in Pompeius Strabo's triumph, surprised Quintus Labienus in the Taurus and defeated the Parthian cavalry that attacked his hill camp; Labienus fled and was killed. Ventidius then beat the Parthian Pharnapates at the Amanus pass and recovered Syria.

sides.strength: Parthian cavalry and Labienus' Roman troops

battle.significance: Expelled the Parthians from Asia Minor and Syria.

events.title: Battle of Gindarus
events.summary: Pacorus invaded Syria again. Ventidius, having fed him false information about his route, waited on high ground near Gindarus; the Parthian cavalry charged uphill into slingers and legionaries and Pacorus was killed. His head was sent round the cities of Syria.
events.detail: Dio says the battle fell on the anniversary of Carrhae. Ventidius, the first Roman to triumph over the Parthians, did so on 27 November 38; Antony, jealous, gave him no further command.

battle.significance: Avenged Carrhae in Roman eyes; killed Parthia's heir.

events.debate: The 9 June date depends on Dio's claim of the Carrhae anniversary.

events.title: Octavian marries Livia
events.summary: Octavian divorced Scribonia, Sextus Pompey's kinswoman, on the day she bore his only child Julia, and married Livia Drusilla, six months pregnant by her husband Tiberius Claudius Nero, who gave her away at the wedding. The marriage, which lasted 51 years, allied him with the Claudii.

events.title: Naval battle off Cumae and the storm of Scyllaeum
events.summary: Sextus' freedman admiral Menas defected to Octavian with Sardinia. In the war that followed Sextus' admiral Menecrates was killed in a sea fight off Cumae, but Octavian was beaten in the straits of Messina and a storm off Scyllaeum wrecked most of his fleet. Octavian had to start again.

battle.significance: Sextus kept control of the sea; Octavian turned to Agrippa to build a new navy.

events.title: Treaty of Tarentum
events.summary: Through Octavia's mediation the triumvirs renewed their powers for a further five years, to the end of 33. Antony gave Octavian 120 ships for the war against Sextus in return for a promise of 20,000 legionaries for Parthia, which Octavian never delivered. Antony returned east and soon after formally acknowledged his twins by Cleopatra.

events.title: Herod and Sosius take Jerusalem
events.summary: With Antony's governor Gaius Sosius and Roman legions, Herod besieged Antigonus in Jerusalem and took it after five months. The Roman troops massacred the population until Herod bought them off. Antigonus, the last Hasmonean king, was sent to Antony and beheaded at Antioch.
events.detail: Josephus claims the city fell on the same day as to Pompey, 27 years before. Herod ruled as Rome's client king until 4 BC.

sides.strength: Sosius' legions and Herod's army, c. 11 legions per Josephus

battle.significance: Ended the Hasmonean dynasty; inaugurated Herodian Judaea.

events.title: Battle of Mylae (36 BC)
events.summary: Agrippa, with the new fleet he had trained in the Portus Julius, a harbour he created in 37 by cutting Lake Avernus and Lake Lucrinus through to the sea, defeated Sextus' admiral Papias off Mylae. Days later Octavian, landing near Tauromenium, was routed at sea by Sextus and barely escaped.

battle.significance: Agrippa's first sea victory; prelude to Naulochus.

events.title: Battle of Naulochus
events.summary: Some 300 ships a side met off Naulochus. Agrippa's heavier ships used the harpax, a grapnel fired from a catapult and reeled in by winch, to drag enemy ships alongside for boarding. Sextus lost 28 ships sunk and almost all the rest captured, burned or run ashore, escaping with 17 to the East. Agrippa received a naval crown, a golden wreath decorated with ships' prows.
events.detail: Octavian, Suetonius reports, was so deeply asleep before the battle that friends had to wake him to give the signal, a story enemies used to mock his courage. Sextus was captured and executed at Miletus in 35 by Antony's officer Marcus Titius.

battle.significance: Destroyed Sextus' sea power; ended the last Pompeian resistance.

scholarship: Welch, Magnus Pius: Sextus Pompeius and the Transformation of the Roman Republic (2012)

events.title: Lepidus deposed
events.summary: Lepidus, who had brought 14 legions from Africa and received the surrender of Sextus' army, claimed Sicily for himself. Octavian walked into his camp almost alone and the legions deserted to him. Lepidus, in mourning clothes, begged for mercy; he was stripped of his triumviral power but allowed to keep the office of pontifex maximus and lived under guard at Circeii until 13 or 12 BC.
events.detail: Octavian, now master of 40 legions, received the sacrosanctity of a tribune for life and an ovation. Rome would have two masters, not three.

events.title: Antony's Parthian campaign and the siege of Phraaspa
events.summary: Antony invaded Media Atropatene through Armenia with 16 legions and perhaps 100,000 men, leaving his siege train of 300 wagons with two legions under Oppius Statianus. The Parthian king Phraates IV and the Median king destroyed the train and its escort while Artavasdes of Armenia withdrew his cavalry. Unable to take Phraaspa without engines, Antony retreated in October across mountains in 27 days and 18 battles.
events.detail: Plutarch puts the losses at 20,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry, half to disease, with 8,000 more dying of cold on the march through Armenia to the sea. Antony decimated cohorts that fled. Cleopatra brought clothing and money to Leuke Kome. Octavian's propaganda made the failure, and Antony's dependence on Cleopatra, a central theme.

sides.strength: 16 legions, 10,000 Gallic and Spanish horse, allies; c. 100,000 (Plutarch)
sides.losses: c. 24,000 in the retreat plus c. 8,000 on the march home; 10,000 with the siege train

battle.significance: Antony's military reputation was badly damaged; the East was not conquered.

events.debate: Site of Phraaspa (near Maragheh or Takht-e Soleyman); size of Antony's army.

events.title: Octavian's Illyrian war: the siege of Metulum
events.summary: To give his legions work and himself military glory, Octavian campaigned in Illyricum in 35-33. At Metulum, capital of the Iapydes, he was wounded when a siege bridge collapsed; the defenders burned the town and themselves. He took Siscia on the Save and later recovered standards lost by Gabinius in 48.

battle.significance: Gave Octavian a military record to set against Antony's.

events.title: The Donations of Alexandria
events.summary: After capturing Artavasdes of Armenia, Antony staged a triumph-like procession in Alexandria and then, on silver thrones in the gymnasium, proclaimed Cleopatra Queen of Kings and Caesarion, as Caesar's true son, King of Kings. Alexander Helios was given Armenia, Media and Parthia (yet to be conquered), Cleopatra Selene Cyrenaica and Libya, and the infant Ptolemy Philadelphus Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia.
events.detail: Coins of Antony and Cleopatra hail her as queen of kings and of her sons who are kings. In Rome the proclamation of Caesarion directly challenged Octavian's status as Caesar's son, and the celebration of a 'triumph' outside Rome was presented as treason.

events.title: Agrippa's aedileship
events.summary: Though a former consul, Agrippa took the junior office of aedile and spent lavishly on the city: he repaired the aqueducts and built the Aqua Julia, sailed through the Cloaca Maxima on a boat after cleaning it, set up 700 basins and 105 fountains, and provided free baths, barbers, oil and lotteries. It was a campaign to win the urban plebs for Octavian.

events.title: The rupture of 32: Antony's will and the oath of Italy
events.summary: When the consuls Sosius and Ahenobarbus attacked Octavian in the senate, he came with armed men; the consuls and over 300 senators fled to Antony. Antony divorced Octavia. Plancus and Titius defected and revealed Antony's will, which Octavian seized illegally from the Vestals and read to the senate: it recognised Caesarion, left legacies to Cleopatra's children and asked for burial in Alexandria.
events.detail: The whole of Italy then swore an oath of personal allegiance to Octavian, followed by the western provinces; Augustus later claimed in the Res Gestae that 'all Italy swore in my words of its own accord'. Some 700 senators fought on his side. The legality of Octavian's position after the triumvirate lapsed is murky; this oath was its substitute.

events.title: War declared on Cleopatra
events.summary: Octavian had war declared on Cleopatra alone, not Antony, to frame the coming civil war as a foreign war. He performed the archaic fetial rite himself, hurling a bloodied spear into a plot of 'enemy' ground by the temple of Bellona. Antony was stripped of his consulship for 31 and his powers.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.summary: Antony and Cleopatra's fleet, bottled up in the Ambracian Gulf through summer by Agrippa's blockade and weakened by disease and desertion, came out to break through. After hours of fighting, Cleopatra's squadron of 60 ships hoisted sail and fled through a gap with the war chest; Antony followed in a fast ship. The rest of the fleet fought on and was burned or surrendered; the land army of 19 legions surrendered a week later.
events.detail: Plutarch gives Antony some 230 large warships after burning those he could not crew, and 5,000 dead. That the ships carried their sails, unusual for battle, suggests that escape was planned (Tarn). Agrippa, who had taken Methone and Leucas in the spring, commanded at sea; Octavian's lighter Liburnian ships proved nimbler. Octavian founded Nicopolis on his camp site and built a memorial whose sockets for 35 captured rams survive. The battle became the foundation myth of the regime, embroidered by Virgil and Propertius, though as a fight it was modest.
events.locName: mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, off Actium

sides.strength: c. 400 ships (lighter), 8 legions embarked or ashore
c. 230 warships incl. 60 Egyptian, 19 legions ashore
sides.losses: c. 5,000 killed; fleet and army surrendered

battle.significance: Decided the last civil war of the Republic.

scholarship: Murray & Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)
events.debate: Was Cleopatra's flight treachery, panic or a planned breakout? Most moderns accept a planned breakout, as Tarn argued.

events.title: Fall of Alexandria and death of Antony
events.summary: Octavian advanced on Egypt from Syria while Cornelius Gallus came from Cyrene. Antony won a cavalry skirmish near the hippodrome on 31 July, but the next day his fleet and cavalry went over to Octavian. Told falsely that Cleopatra was dead, he stabbed himself and was hauled up into her mausoleum to die in her arms. 1 August became a holiday at Rome.
events.detail: Octavian's men took Cleopatra alive by a ruse. Antony's son Antyllus was killed at the statue of Caesar where he had taken refuge; Caesarion, lured back from flight towards India, was executed, Octavian's adviser Areius having observed that too many Caesars were not good.

sides.strength: remnant forces; fleet and cavalry defected

battle.significance: Ended the war and the Ptolemaic dynasty.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra
events.summary: Learning that Octavian meant to lead her in his triumph, Cleopatra VII, last Ptolemaic ruler and the last Hellenistic monarch of note, killed herself with her maids Iras and Charmion, probably about 10 or 12 August. The asp brought in a basket of figs is the version Plutarch reports along with others; he admits no one knew the truth, and poison is equally possible.
events.detail: She was 39 and had reigned for 21 years. Octavian, Plutarch says, admired her nobility and buried her beside Antony. In his triumph her effigy was carried with an asp. Her daughter Cleopatra Selene married Juba II of Mauretania.
events.debate: Method of death (asp or poison) and exact date.

events.title: Annexation of Egypt
events.summary: Egypt became a Roman possession under an equestrian prefect answerable to Octavian; senators and leading equites were forbidden to enter it without his permission. Its first prefect, the poet-soldier Gaius Cornelius Gallus, crushed a revolt in the Thebaid and boasted of it on a trilingual stele at Philae (29), and fell from favour and killed himself in 26.
events.detail: Ptolemaic treasure paid off Octavian's armies and the land bought for veterans; interest rates at Rome fell from 12 to 4 per cent, Dio says. Egypt's grain fed Rome for centuries. Octavian visited Alexander's tomb, accidentally breaking the nose of the mummy, and declined to see the Ptolemies, saying he had come to see a king, not corpses.

events.title: Marcus Crassus denied the spolia opima
events.summary: Marcus Licinius Crassus, grandson of the triumvir and proconsul of Macedonia, killed Deldo, king of the Bastarnae, with his own hands and claimed the right to dedicate the spolia opima to Jupiter Feretrius, the rarest honour in Roman arms. He was refused, it seems because he did not hold independent command; Livy reports that Augustus produced the linen corslet of Cossus proving that only a consul could claim it.
events.detail: Crassus triumphed in 27 but disappeared from public life. Historians see the episode as Octavian refusing to let any other general outshine him.
events.debate: Whether the corslet story was fabricated for the occasion.

events.title: Octavian's triple triumph
events.summary: On 13, 14 and 15 August Octavian triumphed over Illyricum, Actium and Egypt; in the Egyptian procession Cleopatra's effigy with the asp and her children Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene were displayed. He dedicated the temple of the Deified Julius on 18 August, its speakers' platform adorned with rams from Actium, and the rebuilt senate house, the Curia Julia, with an altar and statue of Victory, on 28 August. The doors of the temple of Janus had been closed earlier that year, signalling peace throughout the empire for the first time since 235.

events.title: Census of 28 and the restoration of laws
events.summary: As consuls with Agrippa, Octavian held the first census in 42 years, registering 4,063,000 citizens, and purged the senate, removing perhaps 190 members. He annulled the illegal measures of the triumviral period by edict from the end of 28, and an aureus of that year proclaims that he restored to the Roman people their laws and rights.
events.detail: The leap from 910,000 in 70/69 to over 4 million is among the most debated numbers in ancient demography: either women and children were now counted (the 'low count', Beloch and Brunt) or Italy's free population was far larger than usually thought (the 'high count', Lo Cascio).
events.debate: Low count versus high count of the Italian population.

events.title: The settlement of 27 BC
events.summary: On 13 January 27 Octavian, consul for the seventh time, announced to the senate that he was returning the res publica to the senate and people. In the choreographed response the senate pressed on him a ten-year command over a large provincia including Spain, Gaul, Syria and Egypt, where most of the legions were, while the other provinces were governed by proconsuls chosen by lot. He was voted the oak-leaf civic crown for his door and laurels for its posts.
events.detail: In the Res Gestae (34) he claims that from then on he exceeded all others in auctoritas but had no more power (potestas) than his colleagues in each magistracy. A golden shield in the Curia (a marble copy survives at Arles) praised his virtue, clemency, justice and piety. Ovid dates the restoration of the provinces to the Ides of January. Syme's verdict that the Republic was 'restored' as a façade over a military monarchy set the modern debate; others stress the genuine attempt to rebuild consensus.
events.debate: Restored republic or veiled monarchy? Debate on what 'res publica restituta' meant to contemporaries.

events.title: Octavian receives the name Augustus
events.summary: Three days later, on the motion of Lucius Munatius Plancus, the senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, 'the revered one', with associations of augury and sanctity. He had considered Romulus but rejected it for its overtones of kingship and fratricide. The date is conventionally taken as the end of the Republic and the start of the Principate.
